x: Introduction Magpie is a storage engine written in Crow. Every write enters an ordered log, kept as a directory of files written once, and a program reads that one history in the ways an application needs: the newest row of each key, the rows since a position, a window, a search ranked as Lucene ranks it, the nearest vectors, an aggregate pushed below the reader and an as-of join. A sequencer orders every write of a process and refuses a stale commit; a merge folds the files into sorted segments; a second node follows the log by its files; and doors let other programs' clients in, over HTTP and in Kafka's and Redis's protocols. Every answer is the same in crow run -i and crow run . Introducing Magpie tells the idea and the design with diagrams, and the first measurements. This book is the manual: Part I, the log : installing Magpie, then a tour of its writes and reads, each a program with what it prints. Part II, other clients : the HTTP door, and the Kafka and Redis protocols Magpie speaks. Part III, built on Magpie : a knowledge graph and a feature store, two packages whose data are Magpie logs. Part IV, reference : every function and part, and each part at work alone. Appendices : the design and the decisions behind it, the port of Magpie's Rust kernels to Crow, how its numbers were measured, and its license. Every program in Parts I and II runs as it is written. crow test --book , run from the repository's root, runs each one interpreted and compiled and holds both to the output printed under it; the parts' programs in Part IV run the same way in the package's example.co .

Installing Magpie Magpie is a Crow package. A program names it among its dependencies, in its crowfile: deps = map[magpie = 'github.com/agncrow/magpie/packages/magpie@v0.1.1'] crow install checks the package out into crow_modules/magpie , and crow.lock pins the commit it took and the hash of the files it installed. A program imports it and calls it qualified; the doors are the package's parts: use magpie, frame use magpie.kafka Magpie needs Crow 0.8.0 or later ( installing Crow ). It stands on the standard library's own layer — use sys for bytes, files and sockets, use memory for the sequencer's state, which the process holds — as any package that needs it may. Its file format is its own ( the design ). The knowledge graph and the feature store are packages of the same repository, installed the same way ( packages/kg , packages/features ); each names magpie in its own crowfile, so crow install puts it beside them.

A second node A second node follows the log: it holds the same files and reads them with the same verbs. A table too large for one node is split into logs by a key, one on each node, and a query runs the same verbs on each and stacks the answers. use magpie --- the leader: its log served to followers, forever served = magpie.share['orders', 3700] use magpie --- a follower, on another machine: the files it lacks, fetched; then --- the log read by position as any log is, and the pass run again seen = -1 came = magpie.follow['orders', 'leader.local', 3700] rows = magpie.since['orders', seen + 1]

kg A knowledge graph written in Crow over Magpie ( use magpie ): nodes and edges as two logs under a root, with history, a graph as of any position, a node's edges read as one key's run, breadth-first walks and paths, patterns matched as joins, rules that derive edges, and a subgraph handed to the graph package for pagerank, components and shortest paths. Each answers the same in crow run -i and crow run . deps = map[kg = 'github.com/agncrow/magpie/packages/kg@v0.1.1'] crow install checks the package out into crow_modules/kg , and the package it is written over, magpie, beside it; crow.lock pins the commit each took and the hash of the files it installed. A program imports it and calls it qualified: use magpie, frame use kg The logs A graph lives under a root directory as three Magpie logs (a fourth, vectors , once a node is embedded: see embed ). nodes is keyed by id and holds label , props (JSON text), gone and at ; edges is keyed by src , rel , dst and holds weight , source (provenance: where the fact came from), gone and at ; back holds every edge again keyed by dst , rel , src . Each log's time column is at , in milliseconds. A merged segment of edges is sorted by src , so a node's out-edges are one run of one row group, and back makes its in-edges one too. A graph of a billion edges is read a node at a time; the whole of a small one is edges[root] . Writes node[root, id, label = '', props = '{}', at = -1] writes a node and answers its position; retire[root, id, at = -1] writes its tombstone. link[root, src, rel, dst, weight = 1.0, origin = '', at = -1] writes an edge forward and back and answers its position in edges ; unlink[root, src, rel, dst, at = -1] its tombstone in both. at is the moment the fact holds from; -1 is now. A write is a Magpie put : visible to the process at once, durable at the log's next flush (or at once with sync[dir] of the log). rule[root, f, at = -1] applies a rule: f takes the edges as a frame and answers a frame of src , rel , dst — the edges it derives — which are linked with source 'rule'; it answers how many it linked. A rule runs over the whole graph, so it is for a graph that fits a frame; extraction from text is the llm module writing triples with link . Reads Every read takes upto , a position of the edges log (or the nodes log): the graph as it stood then; -1 is now. A read skips tombstones. nodes[root, upto = -1] , edges[root, upto = -1] : the newest row of each node, of each edge — the whole graph. neighbors[root, id, rel = '', upto = -1] : a node's out-edges, by one relation or all; inbound[root, id, rel = '', upto = -1] its in-edges, each as the edge is written ( src , rel , dst ). history[root, id, upto = -1] : every version of a node's out-edges, oldest first, the tombstones among them. walk[root, origin, hops, rel = '', upto = -1] : the nodes within hops edges, breadth first, as a frame of id , hops and via (the node each was reached from). path[root, a, b, hops = 6, rel = '', upto = -1] : the path of the fewest edges, as the ids along it; an empty list where none. match[root, s, r, o, upto = -1] : a pattern as three lists — subjects, relations, objects, a triple each — where a name beginning with ? is a variable: a frame with a column per variable and a row per way the pattern holds. Each triple's edges are read as neighbors or inbound reads them (the whole graph where the triple names no node), and the triples are joined on the variables they share, so every triple after the first shares one with an earlier triple, and a variable appears once in a triple. subgraph[root, ids, upto = -1] : the edges among the nodes, as a frame of a , b , rel , weight — what the graph package's of_edges takes, an Edge[a, b, weight] per row. asof[root, f, columns = []] : the edges as they stood at each row's moment — f holds src , rel , dst and at — Magpie's prior over the edges log. embed[root, id, v, at = -1] : a node's embedding written to the vectors log (a column of vectors, keyed by the id; a node re-embedded has a newer version); similar[root, v, k = 10, upto = -1] : the k nodes whose newest embedding lies nearest the vector by the cosine, as id and score , the best first — Magpie's nearest , exact, the stale versions dropped — so an entity is found by meaning and the edges expand it. use magpie, frame use kg p = kg.node['people', 'alice', 'person', '{"title": "engineer"}'] p = kg.link['people', 'alice', 'works_at', 'acme', 1.0, 'crm'] staff = kg.inbound['people', 'acme', 'works_at'] near = kg.walk['people', 'alice', 2] who = kg.match['people', ['?x', '?x'], ['knows', 'works_at'], ['?y', 'acme']] Held to main.co 's test blocks: the two logs and their tombstones, a read as of a position, a node's history, a walk and a path against a graph drawn by hand, the patterns' joins, a rule's edges, a subgraph, and the edges as of a moment; example.co runs interpreted and compiled under ./test.sh with one output. features A feature store written in Crow over Magpie ( use magpie ): a feature group is a log keyed by its entity with its event-time column declared, so one write is both stores — the history for training is the log, the newest value per entity for serving is the sequencer's image — and there is no materialisation job between them. A feature's definition is one Crow function, run over windows for the backfill and over the log's tail for the stream. A training set is the labels joined against each group's history as of each label's moment. The registry is a log of its own. Each answers the same in crow run -i and crow run , and training answers what pandas's merge_asof answers. deps = map[features = 'github.com/agncrow/magpie/packages/features@v0.1.1'] crow install checks the package out into crow_modules/features , and the package it is written over, magpie, beside it; crow.lock pins the commit each took and the hash of the files it installed. A program imports it and calls it qualified: use magpie, frame use features A group is a log declare[dir, entity, time] names a group: the log at dir , keyed by the entity's columns ( ['user'] , or several), each row's moment in the column time (milliseconds, or a column of moments). It answers a Group record and writes nothing; the first append declares the log so (Magpie's keys and time column, declared once). append[g, f] appends feature rows — the entity's columns, the time column and the features — through Magpie's put : visible to online at once, durable at the log's next flush ( sync of the log, for at once). A _pos column a read left on the rows is dropped. It answers the first position the rows took. Two reads, one log online[g, key] : the newest feature row of one entity (its key's values, each as text), from the image Magpie's sequencer keeps in memory — the online store's read, in microseconds; a frame of one row, or of none. history[g, from = 0, upto = -1, columns = []] : a window of the group's history by position — the offline store, read a window at a time, with the columns named. One function for the backfill and the stream A feature function takes a frame of source rows and answers a frame of feature rows (the entity's columns, the time column, the features): fn spend[rows] out = select[rows, ['user', 'at']] out.big = rows.amount gt 50.0 out.cents = rows.amount * 100.0 return out backfill[g, source, f, from = 0, upto = -1, per = 100000] runs it over the source log in windows of per positions and appends what it answers, and answers how many rows it wrote. stream[g, source, f, after, seconds] runs the same function over the source's tail — the rows past after , waited for up to the seconds — and answers the last position taken, the loop's next after ( after itself where none came). The same rows come out of either path: a feature computed one way for training and another for serving has no place to arise. A function that needs a row's past reads it with online (the entity's newest row) or history . A training set is the labels as of their moments training[labels, groups, columns = [], upto = -1] joins the labels — the entity's columns and a moment in the groups' time column — against each group: beside each label, the group's newest row at or before the label's moment (by time, then by position; missing cells where none precedes), the labels' columns first. columns names the features taken from each group, every column the labels lack when none is named. The labels carry a column named as each group's time column. It is Magpie's prior per group, read from each key's run in the key-sorted segments and the tail, the history never held as one frame. upto is the position the set is as of (-1 is now): a dataset a position names comes out the same at every run. Embeddings are features A column of vectors is a feature like any other: append writes it (from a matrix or a list of vectors), online serves the entity's newest embedding, training joins it as of each label's moment, and similar[g, column, v, k = 10] answers the entities whose embedding lies nearest a vector by the cosine (Magpie's nearest , exact), the group's rows with a score , the best first. Freshness and the registry freshness[g] answers a frame of one row: head (the log's last position), rows and newest (the time column's largest value written), from the log's figures and a summary pushed below the reader. define[dir, feature, g, meaning, computed = '', at = -1] registers a feature — its name, its group's log, entity and time column, what it means and which function computes it — in the registry log at dir , keyed by the feature's name; defined[dir] answers every feature's newest definition, and the log keeps their history. The log: use magpie Import with use magpie ; every function is called qualified ( magpie.put[…] ). The log as a directory of batch files, written in Crow on the sys layer (design rule 20): each commit is one file, written once (magpie.merger's write_batch , the sequencer's flush) — a frame given a position per row in a column _pos , its rows sorted by the key columns, in row groups of a few megabytes, and in the file's index the statistics a reader prunes by per column per group (min, max, the missing and distinct counts and a bloom filter, a filter over the words of each text column indexed), read on demand: a reader of two columns of a thousand reads two columns' index and two columns' chunks. The file is Magpie's own format (magpie.fileformat; docs/magpie-design.md, phase 2), no library's. Every write of a process goes through its sequencer ( put , batch , commit ): the rows are visible to the process at once and durable at the flush, and latest of one key ( equal ) reads its newest row from the image in memory. One file is at once the log entry (positions), the level-0 segment (sorted, with statistics) and the search index (word filters, and the counts a search's scoring reads). The numbering, the sequencer, the reads, the search and the catalog's state are the package's; a log is a directory path, a snapshot a position. Design Note: a manifest, and keys declared once. Considered: the directory as the catalog, as the first architecture had — every read listed the log and read every file's head to decide what to open (rejected 2026-10-26: the listing was the index, a merge's switch was two steps a crash could split, and nothing said which files were live); keys given at every call — batch[d, f, by = …] , merge[d, by = …] , latest[d, by] (rejected: a log sorted by one key at write and merged by another is a mess nobody wants, and latest by a column that is no key is a group over scan , in Crow); a second declared sort order, so a reverse-edges log for a graph would be the merge's work (rejected for now: a second order is a second log the program writes, two batch calls, and a package over Magpie does that; a declared order would double every merge for every log). Considered: a query engine linked, as DataFusion (rejected 2026-10-26, Vijay's rule: nothing third-party in Magpie); a planner and a vectorised executor of our own, with a query vocabulary in Crow to drive it (rejected as a phase: a multi-year engine, and the boundary stated under what Magpie does not do). Not here: joins of two large logs in one plan, subqueries, window functions — loops over windows in Crow. Design Note: search's long tail, in our own code. Considered: Lucene's engine linked, as tantivy (rejected 2026-10-26, Vijay's rule: nothing third-party in Magpie). Design Note: reads bounded by what a frame holds. Considered: a read that answers a stream, so a billion rows could be walked by one call (rejected 2026-10-26: the language has one shape for rows, a frame, and a stream of frames is the loop the program writes). Decided: every read is bounded — since and scan by a position window, latest by a range of the log's first key, lookup and search by their keys and k — and a read over the whole log is a loop over windows in Crow, each window reading its segments and its columns and nothing else; an aggregate over the whole log stays such a loop until the executor of phase 8 pushes the common ones below the reader. Design Note: indexes built by the merge, never by the producer. Considered: the producer naming the columns to index ( texts on batch , as the first architecture had; rejected 2026-10-26, Vijay's question: an ingestion job should not know what will be asked of its rows, and a column it did not name was unsearchable until the log was rewritten); every batch indexing every text column (rejected: the price on the write path for columns never searched, and the decision still at ingestion). Decided: the merge indexes every text column of every segment it writes, per row group, giving a column up where its distinct tokens exceed half its documents (an identifier column: a filter of every value prunes nothing); a search reads an indexed group through its filter and any other group whole, and scores both the same, so a row is searchable the moment it lands, cheap once merged, and no producer decides either. A batch's own words are not indexed: the tail is small because the merge runs. Design Note: the streaming merge and its levels. Considered: every merge folding every file into one segment, as the first architecture had (rejected 2026-10-26: the merge stacked every live file into one frame, sorted it and wrote the segment into one buffer — it ended at RAM — and every merge rewrote the whole log); segments in position order with blooms alone for the keys (rejected: it gives up the one-group lookup by the keys a segment is sorted by, the thing the measure showed); key-ordered levels with disjoint ranges, as LevelDB keeps them (rejected: a log compacts by time, and disjoint key ranges make since read every segment). Decided: a k-way merge over inputs that are already sorted by the keys then position, one row group per input and one for the output in memory, the newest version of a key the last of its run; segments of at most a gigabyte, named by a counter since a merge that splits by size makes two over one position range; levels with a fan-out of eight, the tail folding into level 1 and a level's oldest eight into the next, so a merge touches a slice and a billion rows are a few dozen segments; across segments the newest position wins at read, which lookup and latest already do. Design Note: Magpie's own file format. Considered: Arrow IPC for a batch and Parquet for a segment, as the first architecture had, the statistics as one JSON text in the file's head (rejected 2026-10-26: no third-party code in Magpie — Vijay's rule; and three costs of their own: the head was parsed whole by every query of any column, tens of megabytes at a thousand columns; Parquet keeps a footer entry per column per row group, so a billion rows in groups of 8192 was the known wide-table pathology; every write converted the frame to Arrow and every read converted it back). Decided: one format for a batch, a segment and the manifest, designed around the frame's columns — a chunk is a column's cells over a row group as the frame holds them, encoded by its kind; the index is per column, found through a two-level footer, so a reader reads the one column's one group; the codec is our own, applied where it pays. Design Note: the oldest protocol every client speaks. Considered: the current protocol (record batches of magic 2 — varints, CRC-32C, headers, compression — and flexible request versions with tagged fields) (rejected for the first door: a client reads the broker's ApiVersions and speaks what it says, so a door that says 0.10.1 is spoken to in legacy message sets, a fixed layout with one checksum, by every client written since — the pure-Python client, librdkafka's, the Java one — and the record kernel is a page where the current format is a chapter; the current format is the door's next step, behind the same records rows). Considered: a thread per connection (rejected: the interpreter runs later inline, so a door that spawned would serve one client at a time interpreted and many compiled — the two modes must run the same way — and a Kafka client opens several connections at once: one for metadata, one per broker, one for its group's coordinator; one loop polling each connection, waiting five milliseconds at a time, serves them all the same way in both modes). A topic's one partition is the magpie's one log; partitions would be logs under the topic, and are not made until a client asks for them. Magpie: the design (Moved here from the crow repository's docs/ on 2026-10-30, when Magpie became a repository of its own: a path below that names crow's sources — src/ , crow_runtime/ , tests/parity/ , the Rust tests — is the crow repository's, as it was when written; Magpie's own files are this repository's packages/ , examples/ and tests/ .) Written 2026-10-26, before any of it is built. Magpie is the data platform that was built as lake (phases 0–6 of the first architecture, commits c642869 → 61c20d9): one store that takes the stream, holds the table, indexes the text, keeps the current state and orders the transactions, in one process, written in Crow on the sys layer with kernels in Rust. The first architecture holds at tens of millions of rows and was never released. (Since 2026-10-28 the kernels this note describes in Rust are Crow — each ported and held to the Rust kernel's bytes, then the Rust deleted: docs/magpie-in-crow.md. Where this note says a kernel does something, the Crow module of that name does it now, the same way. And since 2026-10-29 Magpie is a package, packages/magpie , its modules the package's parts under the names of its files — tail is sequencer , merge merger , file fileformat , encode columnchunk , codec lz77 , packing bitpack , stem stemmer , exec executor , search searcher , nearest knn , records recordsets — called qualified, as a package is: magpie.latest[…] , kafka.serve[…] .) Vijay's decisions, 2026-10-26: The name is magpie : the corvid that gathers everything into one nest. lake goes entirely (no alias, no message: a retired name is an unknown name). The Kafka door keeps its name, kafka . Nothing is released until the architecture holds at a billion rows and a thousand columns on one machine, and until the four capabilities it stands in for — an analytics engine, a search index, a current-state store, a transactional store — are its own, at their engines' cost class, verified by measure. All of it is Crow or our own Rust. No third-party code in Magpie: its files are its own format, written straight from the frame's columns, with its own encodings and its own codec; the Kafka door decodes gzip and snappy with our own decoders. flate2 and snap leave crow_runtime. arrow and parquet stay for the frame module ( frame_of_parquet , the web's Arrow responses) and are not Magpie's: a program that wants a segment as Parquet exports it through a frame. The compiler is untouched (design rule 24). Anything new is a module, a row, a kernel, or a runtime component. The spec's section ( docs/language-spec.md , magpie) is updated as each phase lands; this note records what was decided and why. Phases are in build order; each is one gated commit series that keeps every test before it and ends with a measure. What is wrong with the first architecture Five things, none of them a verb: The merge is in memory. batch::merge stacks every live file into one frame, sorts, deduplicates and writes the segment into one buffer. It ends at RAM. A file's head is one JSON of every column's statistics , parsed whole by every query of any column. A thousand columns is tens of megabytes per file, read by a lookup that wants one. Magpie in Crow: the kernels rewritten, and what the language gains for it (Moved here from the crow repository's docs/ on 2026-10-30, when Magpie became a repository of its own: a path below that names crow's sources — src/ , crow_runtime/ , tests/parity/ , the Rust tests — is the crow repository's, as it was when written; Magpie's own files are this repository's packages/ , examples/ and tests/ .) (Since 2026-10-29 Magpie is a package, packages/magpie : the modules this note ports are its parts, under its files' names — codec is lz77 , packing bitpack , encode columnchunk , file fileformat , tail sequencer , merge merger , exec executor , search searcher , nearest knn , stem stemmer , records recordsets — and their tests run from there: crow test packages/magpie/lz77.co .) Decided by Vijay, 2026-10-27: a package is written in Crow, and its author writes no Rust. Magpie is the first package held to that rule, and it is the hardest case, because two thirds of it is Rust today: the kernels under crow_runtime/src/magpie/ (7,500 lines: the file format, the codec, the encodings, the merge, the sequencer, the executor, the postings and the search, the nearest scan, the bloom filters, the gzip and snappy decoders, the stemmer) and the Kafka records kernel ( crow_runtime/src/kafka.rs ), reached from the Crow modules through nineteen rows of the sys layer. This document is the plan to rewrite every one of them in Crow, held to the Rust original as the oracle, and the five things the language lacks for that, each checked against the spec for an existing way (design rules 1 and 24). What stays Rust is the language's own: frames, tensors, text, sockets, the core pool, the compiler. crow_runtime keeps its kernels; a package gets none. 1. The rule, and what it costs A kernel written in Crow runs at the interpreter's speed under crow run -i and at the compiled program's under crow run . For per-byte work the interpreter is two orders slower than Rust, so a package's kernels must be compiled ahead of the programs that use them: the assembly step of the package plan (docs/magpie-repo-design, to be written) compiles the functions a crowfile names and registers them as rows the interpreter calls natively, so both modes run the same compiled code. Until assembly exists, Magpie's kernels inside the standard module run interpreted under crow run -i : correct, held by the same tests, and slow. The measures in docs/magpie-design.md are re-run in compiled mode at the end of the port and the interpreted numbers stated as they are, which is the case for assembly. Compiled Crow over bytes and ints is the evidence the port stands on: revcomp, k-nucleotide and fasta run within a small factor of Rust, after the emitter's work on text builders, plain vectors and known-ASCII reads. The CSV parser that measured 20 to 45 times slower than the runtime's did per-cell work through values that can fail; the primitives below are chosen so a kernel never does that. The first kernel ported is the codec, and it is measured against its Rust original on the same input before the second is begun: if compiled Crow lands within about two times, the port goes on; if not, the emitter is where the work is, not the kernels. 2. What Crow lacks, and the form each takes Every item below was searched for in the spec first. Where a form exists it is extended by kind or by an option, never doubled. 2.1 Bytes written in place What exists: bytes[text] , text[b] , len[b] , byte[b, i] , slice[b, from, to] , find[b, needle] , concat[a, b] , pack , unpack , ieee[x] , hex , hash , digest , hmac , random[n] , mask , xor , same . A bytes value is Bytes(Vec<u8>) in the runtime, held plain in both backends. What a kernel lacks is writing: a decoder builds its output a byte at a time, an encoder writes lengths into what it wrote, a hash table of positions is a vector of ints. bytes[n] : n zero bytes (a second bytes row, by kind, beside bytes[text] ). set[b, i, v] : the byte at i replaced by v , 0 to 255, counted from the end when negative, outside stops (the set the lists and maps have, for bytes). push[b, v] : the byte appended (the push the lists have). concat[a, b] with a moved: appended where a lies. All three in place through what exists: Prop::InPlace on the row, a take bridge for the interpreter's moved argument, a taken path the emitter prints when the first argument is a moved local ( taken_in_place splits b = set[b, i, byte[b, j]] as it splits a list's). Reads stay byte[b, i] : a kernel's loop reads and writes by position, and the vector of ints a hash table needs is a one-axis tensor, which the emitter already keeps as Vec<i64> . 2.2 Numbers in bytes What exists: pack[n, width] and unpack[b, at, width] are big-endian and signed, as Kafka's wire is; ieee[x] is a float's eight bytes, big-endian. Magpie's format is little-endian with unsigned lengths, and a decoder reads floats. pack[n, width, little = false] , unpack[b, at, width, little = false, signed = true] : the options, defaults as today. ieee[x, width = 8, little = false] , and ieee[b, at, width, little] : the bytes at at as the float they spell (a second ieee row, by kind, the inverse of the first), 4 for single precision; the reader's width and byte order are positions, since an option may be given by position and ieee[b, at, 8] would be the writer's row with a width and a byte order. digest[b, 'crc32'] and hash[b, 'crc32'] : the checksum gzip and Kafka's message sets carry, four bytes, written by us as the other digests are not (a table-driven CRC-32 is twenty lines; the spec's "what stays native" note names no crate for it). wrapmul[a, b] , wrapadd[a, b] , wrapsub[a, b] in use bits : the product, sum or difference of two 64-bit patterns wrapped to 64 bits, the int of the low bits. A hash (FNV's multiply per byte, murmur's mix), a linear congruence and a checksum are written on wrapping arithmetic, which a language whose ints grow has no way to say: the product of two ints past 2^32 is a growing int, exact and slow, and bitand of it with a 64-bit mask is a growing int's operation too. The three rows answer a 64-bit int, so the width pass keeps what is computed from them narrow. What the width pass needs from a kernel's loop, found porting the codec and the packing: bits gather by bitor , never by + , since a sum in a loop is a growing int to the pass and bitor of two non-negative ints is bounded by the larger's power of two; a value wider than 32 bits is packed as its low 32 bits and its high bits apart, so no shift passes 64 bits; and a 64-bit pattern at or past 2^63 is held as the negative int of the same bits, assembled as lo + shift[hi, 32] where hi is read as signed in a branch the pass bounds. CROW_WIDTH_DEBUG=1 shows the settled ranges; a kernel is not done while one of its loop's ints is wide. 2.3 Files What exists: file[path] (bytes, whole), store[path, bytes] , filesize[path] , read , write , exists , mkdir , ls , rm . The write path of a batch is: write a part file, flush it to the disk, link it into place (never over an existing name), flush the directory. A reader opens a file's footer, then one chunk. The footer cache is keyed by path, size and modification time. file[path, from, n] : the bytes of a region (a third file row, by arity). modified[path] : when the file was last written, a moment. flushed[path] : the file, or the directory, written through to the disk ( F_FULLFSYNC on macOS, fsync elsewhere); answers the path. link[from, to] : a hard link, refused with the system's reason where to exists; answers to . move[from, to] : renamed over to , atomically, as a manifest is replaced; answers to . ( rename is the frame module's.) 2.4 Process memory What exists: top-level variables, invisible to functions; facts, a served app's state, typed by their declaration and held by the session layer; env ; the notes a connection keeps ( note , noted : text, per stream). Nothing a module's functions can hold between calls for the process, shared by its threads. The sequencer is that: the rows put since the last flush, the key index, the image of each key's newest row; so is the footer cache, and the registry of what a process has opened. remember[name, v] : the value held for the process under the name, replacing what was held. recall[name, default] : the value held, or the default where none is; typed by the default, as env[name, default] is answered by its default's shape. forget[name] : nothing held under the name. revise[name, default, f, x] : f[held, x] run under the name's lock, with held the value held (the default where none), the value f answers held afterwards and answered; f owns the value it is handed, so a map's insert or a list's push inside it is in place. One schedule at a time per name, so two handlers writing one log serialise by construction, as the Rust sequencer's lock serialises them. The store is per process and per mode: the compiled program keeps typed slots, the interpreter its values; the semantics are one. Two effect kinds carry the rules: held for a read, held.write for the rest, allowed and refused where db.read and db.write are (a view reads neither; a derivation reads, never writes), ordered in a loop for the writes, recorded by no rehearsal since nothing leaves the program. One kind of the row vocabulary is new: Kind::Any , the kind of the argument handed where it is taken, which types recall 's answer by its default and revise 's function by its default and the rest of its arguments, as later[f, a, b] hands its rest to f . Design Note, recorded here for the spec: a timer was considered for the sequencer's flush and rejected again (the spec's "Periodicity Is Declared, Not Written"). A put appends to the process's memory and schedules later[flush_all] , with no argument, which is allowed in a handler too: coalesced, so a burst of puts shares one flush; waited for at exit, so nothing put is lost to a clean end; run inline by the interpreter, so under crow run -i a put is durable when it answers, which is a legal schedule and a slower one. The ten milliseconds of the Rust thread become "as soon as the loop is free". 2.5 Columns as their parts What exists: a loop over a column yields its cells, each a value that can fail where the cell can be missing; df.name reads a column and df.name = values writes one from a list, a tensor or a column; a frame's columns . What the writer and the reader of a file do instead is read a column's rows start..end as the vectors they are held in and build a column from such vectors, with no value per cell: the Rust writer encodes Vec<i64> and a validity bitmap; the reader hands the frame a Column it decoded whole. The CSV parser's factor came from the per-cell path, and the file format's chunk is the vector's shape. Rows of the sys layer, each over a column and a range of its rows, answering what a chunk holds: ints_of[col, from, to] (missing as 0), floats_of , bools_of , millis_of and zones_of for a moment column, vectors_of (the rows' floats laid flat) with vector_width[col] , text_bytes_of with text_ends_of (each cell's end offset, as the text is held), present_of (the validity as a bitmap's bytes, bit i of byte i / 8, the chunk's own layout, empty where every cell is present), and cell_kind[col] ( int , float , text , bool , moment , vector ). The inverse builds a column from its parts: ints_column[ints, present] , floats_column , bools_column[bits, present] , moments_column[millis, zones, present] , vectors_column[width, floats, present] , text_column[bytes, ends, present] , each a Column the program writes onto a frame with df. name = … , which exists. A distinct count is exact: a map keyed by a 64-bit hash of the cell's bytes holding the byte strings that share it, compared with same . 2.6 Parallel decoding Nothing new. A loop over file reads is ordered, since a read is an effect; a kernel reads the groups it needs first, then decodes them in a loop with no effect, which the compiler runs across the cores. 2.7 Packages and the sys layer use sys had been refused in a program and allowed in a standard module. A package that holds kernels needs it: bytes, files, hashing, memory. Proposed: a package's parts may use sys . Decided wider (Vijay, 2026-10-29): keeping sys and memory to the standard library is a suggestion, not a rule — any program or package may import them, and a package that needs a kernel's speed is written on them. 3. What the measures found, each fixed with its test: The sequencer flushed one put at a time. A flush wrote and synced its file inside revise , holding the tail's lock, and a put waits on that lock: each put waited out the last one's fsync, then asked a flush of its own row (2,000 files of one row; 61 s of system time). The kernel held the lock for its write too, but flushed from a timer every 10 ms, so puts gathered between flushes. Now the flush claims the pending parts under the lock, writes them outside it and lets them go under it ( _claimed , _written , _settled ): the puts that arrive during a write join the next flush, with no timer. The write goes to a file of the claim's own, linked into the batch's name under the lock only while the claim holds ( _committed ): rm forgets the tail before it removes the directory, so a log removed while its flush ran keeps none of its rows.
